## Are older insect lineages more species rich in Hawai\`i?

- 700,000 years

::::

Native *Drosophila*

- 25 million years

![from: Church and Extavour (2022) Molecular Biology and Evolution, 39](img/drosoph_phylo.png){width="60%"}

::::

## Are older insect lineages more species rich in Hawai\`i? {.t}

Looks like it...a question for \alert{correlation}

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=4, fig.height=3}
hi_insect <- read.csv("data/hembry_etal.csv")
hi_insect$clade_richness <- round(hi_insect$clade_richness)

ggplot(hi_insect, aes(x = clade_age, y = clade_richness)) +
    geom_point() +
    theme_cowplot() +
    xlab("Clade age (my)") + 
    ylab("Number of species")
```

## Are older insect lineages more species rich in Hawai\`i? {.t}

Using product-moment \alert{correlation}, we got a "significant" correlation

```{r}
cor.test(hi_insect$clade_age, hi_insect$clade_richness)
```


## Are older insect lineages more species rich in Hawai\`i? {.t}

The significant correlation means that clade age and number of species have a \alert{predictive} relationship (I could predict one from the other).

How do we actually predict number of species from clade age?

::: columns

:::: column

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=4, fig.height=3, out.width="100%"}
hi_insect <- read.csv("data/hembry_etal.csv")
hi_insect$clade_richness <- round(hi_insect$clade_richness)

ggplot(hi_insect, aes(x = clade_age, y = clade_richness)) +
    geom_point() +
    theme_cowplot() +
    xlab("Clade age (my)") + 
    ylab("Number of species") +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

::::

:::: column

\large
\it A job for \alert{regression}

## Learning Objectives

1. Use linear regression to predict $Y$ based on $X$
2. Test the null hypothesis of slope = 0
3. Display uncertainty in predictions from a linear regression
4. Use diagnostic plots to evaluate if data meet assumptions of regression
